text: It's day two hundred and twelve. You're rowing to school.
Past the traffic lights. Over the parking lot. And straight in through a window on the second floor.
You're late. And you're leaking.
So, what if it rained for three hundred and sixty-five days straight?
Day one is actually nice. The air smells good, football practice is cancelled, and everybody stays in bed.
It's just rain. And by the way, falling raindrops don't look like tears. They're round, and flat on the bottom, like tiny hamburger buns.
By day three, nobody is smiling. The weather report has one picture on it, and it never changes.
It isn't even a storm. It's just steady, heavy rain. About one centimeter an hour.
That sounds like nothing. But one centimeter an hour, for a whole year, is eighty-eight meters of water. That's a thirty story building.
At first, the ground just drinks it. Soil is like a sponge, full of tiny holes with air inside.
But on day five, the last hole fills up. After that, every single drop has to go somewhere else.
It goes to your street.
Fifteen centimeters of fast water can knock you off your feet. Thirty can float a small car. Sixty can take almost anything with wheels.
On day nine, it takes the coach's car. He loves that car.
Come back! I'm still paying for you!
But wait. Where is all this water coming from? If you squeezed every drop out of the entire sky, it would cover the Earth with only two and a half centimeters.
So this isn't new water. It's the ocean. The sea evaporates, blows over your town, falls on your head, and runs back down to the sea.
It's one giant conveyor belt, and somebody turned it up to maximum.
Which means the sea doesn't even rise. It drops a little. The flood is wherever the rain lands.
Day twenty. Nothing is dry anymore. Mold only needs a day or two on something wet, so it moves in everywhere. Your shoes. Your curtains. Your bread.
Don't eat the green one. Or the other green one.
And then there's the sound. All day and all night, on every roof in the city. After a while, you stop hearing it. Somehow, that's worse.
On day thirty-four, the water comes in through the front door without knocking.
First the rug floats. Then the sofa. Then the fridge, because a fridge is basically a boat full of cheese.
You carry everything upstairs. The cat carries itself.
Then the lights go out. Power stations are built next to rivers. Now they're inside them.
And here's the cruel part. There's water in every direction, and you can't drink any of it. The drains are flooded, so everything that was down there is up here now.
The only clean water in town is the rain itself. So you put out every pot you own.
Maya lives on the hill. She feels lucky, until day fifty-eight. Wet soil is heavy and slippery, and a hill is just soil that hasn't fallen yet.
At three in the morning, her whole garden slides past the window. With the swing still on it.
Can I come and live on your roof?
So now there are six of you up there. You, your mom, Maya, Maya's mom, her little brother Leo, and a cat who hates everyone.
You build a boat out of two doors and forty empty bottles. Anything floats, if it pushes away enough water. It takes three tries.
By day ninety, it's a town again. Every roof is tied to the next one with rope. There's a floating shop, a floating barber, and a school on the second floor.
Life vests on, people. Yes, even for math.
Food is harder. Roots need air, so in the flooded fields, the wheat drowns standing up.
But some things love it. Rice. Mushrooms. Watercress. And in the old gym, four hundred fish.
Basketball practice still has a net. Just not that kind.
The worst thing isn't the water. It's the gray. A hundred and fifty days without sun, and nobody has a shadow.
Your skin makes vitamin D from sunlight. No sun, and slowly everyone gets tired, and weak, and sad.
What color was the sun?
Nobody knows what to say. So Maya paints one on the ceiling of the classroom. A big one. Leo sits under it every single day.
It has happened before, sort of. One place in Hawaii once had three hundred and thirty-one rainy days in a row.
And two hundred and thirty-two million years ago, the whole planet had a rainy age that lasted more than a million years. A lot of animals didn't make it.
But during it, one small group suddenly spread across the world. The dinosaurs. So rain isn't the end. It's a test.
On day two hundred and five, the radio says the word everyone is afraid of. Dam.
Up the valley, behind one wall of concrete, there's a lake as deep as a twenty story building. Water pushes harder the deeper it gets, and that wall has never been pushed like this.
It was built for the worst storm in a thousand years. Nobody built it for a year with one storm.
Which brings us back to day two hundred and twelve. You climb in through the window. You sit down. You open your soggy book.
And for the first time in seven months, you hear something louder than the rain.
That wasn't thunder.
The dam is gone. A wall of water is coming down the valley, and you have ten minutes.
Everybody yells the same thing. Tie everything down! Get more rope!
But you've been rowing for months, and you know something. A wave doesn't sink a boat. A boat sinks when something is holding it down.
Cut the ropes! Cut all of them!
Your mom cuts one. The coach cuts three. Roof by roof, raft by raft, the whole town comes loose.
Then Maya counts heads. And counts again.
Where's Leo?
He went back for the sun. He's in the classroom, trying to pull it off the ceiling.
You row like you've never rowed before. In through the window. Past the desks. Under the painted sun.
I can't reach it!
You can't save the whole ceiling. But one piece comes loose. He hugs it like a shield, and you go out the other side.
There's one rope left, tied to the school. And the wave is already at the end of the street.
You saw. And you saw. And it snaps.
The raft shoots up. One floor. Two floors. Three. The wave rolls underneath you, and the whole town rises over it like a cork.
All night long, two hundred rafts drift in the dark, calling each other's names.
In the morning, you bump into something hard. A hill. And everybody is on it. Even the coach's car.
I knew you'd wait for me.
After that, people stop waiting for it to end. They plant floating gardens. Babies learn to swim before they can walk. The cat learns to fish.
And Leo carries his sun everywhere. People touch it for luck.
On day three hundred and sixty-five, you wake up early, because something is wrong. It takes you a minute to work out what.
It's quiet.
No drumming on the roof. Nothing. And then a thin line of light walks across the floor, and climbs up your face.
Everybody runs outside. Leo looks down and screams. There's a dark thing stuck to his feet.
It's following me!
It's his shadow. He hasn't seen it in a year.
The water doesn't leave politely. It takes months, and it leaves mud on everything. But flood mud is some of the richest soil on Earth. That spring, the whole valley turns green.
And on every building there's a line, exactly where the water used to be. Kids measure themselves against it.
A year later, it's a normal Tuesday. You're eating cereal. The sun is in the window, and Leo's sun is on the wall.
And then you hear it.
You look at your mom. Your mom looks at you.
It's just the roof.
It's probably just the roof.
Life vests. Now.
